overview: Charrúa here is a cautious cultural label, not a centralized state or an exclusive surveyed border. The imported feature appears only in the atlas’s 1492 snapshot. Its polygon crosses Uruguay, Argentina, and Brazil and, at sampled places, overlaps the atlas labels Bohanes, Guenoa-Muinanes, Tekohá (Guarani), and Moqoit. Those colors disclose editorial reconstruction rather than one government’s surveyed territory. A Museo Nacional de Antropología fascicle separates Charrúa from Guenoa-Minuan and other named peoples, describes territories as changing, and dates its accounts to later settings. It reports riverbank movement, possible canoe use, horse adaptation by about 1640, missions, alliances, conflict, and forced transfers. These later observations follow profound change; they cannot be copied backward into 1492 families or daily routines. This card therefore distinguishes the atlas umbrella from named people and keeps regional archaeology in its own evidentiary lane. Its eight periods are evidence bands rather than annual chronicles. Later language, household, violence, legal, and community sources retain their dates. When the exact feature disappears in 1500, the software changes labels; no source describes a conquest or extinction in that year.

periods.title: A broad atlas label appears
periods.summary: The exact id is absent in 1400 and appears in the 1492 file as one large polygon. Its properties provide an approximate display interval, not a foundation date, ruler list, population count, migration route, or treaty boundary. This first band records the map’s editorial appearance only.

periods.title: Overlaps reveal an umbrella
periods.summary: Salto and Paysandú lie inside both Charrúa and Bohanes layers. Tacuarembó lies inside Charrúa and Guenoa-Muinanes; Rivera and Melo add Tekohá (Guarani). Paraná also overlaps Moqoit. Simultaneous ownership colors make a useful uncertainty warning, not several literal states occupying identical surveyed borders.

periods.title: Names require source criticism
periods.summary: A museum study of the so-called “Charrúa Complex” warns that direct observation is unavailable for early centuries and that historical names may be self-names, outsiders’ names, subdivisions, or different labels for one group. This band marks an identity problem rather than inventing a 1494 event.

periods.title: Regional archaeology supplies context
periods.summary: Stratified shelters, mounds, tools, pottery, and plant remains establish long Indigenous histories within parts of the atlas shape. They do not automatically identify a Charrúa community. Archaeologists must date each context, study its associations, and resist attaching a later ethnic label to every regional object.

periods.title: Written evidence comes later
periods.summary: The first known colonial use of the name Charrúa is in a 1527 account, after this atlas interval. Later records used changing labels from scattered settlements and archives. This evidence band therefore marks a documentary limit instead of pretending that a writer observed a Charrúa community in 1496.

periods.title: Language survives in fragments
periods.summary: Historians of regional linguistics work with sparse word lists, a Guenoa catechism, and later scholars’ disputed classifications. They warn against treating language, ethnicity, and nation as interchangeable. Speech certainly existed in 1497, but no surviving Charrúa-authored text from this atlas interval supplies a grammar or narrative.

periods.title: Bodies do not carry simple labels
periods.summary: Ancient DNA from two people buried at an eastern Uruguayan mound illuminates regional population history. The researchers explicitly caution against equating mound builders with historically named peoples. Genomes can test ancestry relationships; they cannot read the atlas label or assign every burial to Charrúa identity.

periods.title: The software layer ends
periods.summary: The exact feature disappears in the 1500 file, while a broad Pampas layer again covers much of the region. No cited source reports a conquest, collapse, extinction, or border settlement in that year. The map changes categories; people and communities remain outside that software seam.

sections.title: Read the map as an atlas reconstruction

items.text: The target is one Polygon with one ring, 65 stored positions, and 64 unique vertices. Its bounding box runs roughly from 62.03 degrees west to 52.30 degrees west and 35.01 degrees south to 28.93 degrees south. These are decoded file measurements, not Indigenous boundary testimony.

Montevideo, Salto, Paysandú, Tacuarembó, Rivera, Melo, Rocha, Maldonado, Paraná, Santa Fe, and Rosario fall inside the polygon. Colonia, Buenos Aires, Corrientes, Córdoba, Porto Alegre, Pelotas, Florianópolis, and Asunción fall outside. A coarse shape can include one nearby city and miss another.

Rivera and Melo sit beneath three simultaneous atlas labels: Charrúa, Guenoa-Muinanes, and Tekohá (Guarani). Paraná combines Charrúa, Guenoa-Muinanes, and Moqoit. These overlaps expose compilation choices. They cannot be converted into triple taxation, shared capitals, or a population map for 1492.

The 1400 file mostly assigns sampled points to Pampas Cultures or Savanna Hunter-Gatherers. The 1492 file inserts Charrúa and overlapping named layers; the 1500 file removes the exact id and restores a broad Pampas label. This is a cartographic relabeling sequence, not eight years of state formation and collapse.

The import registry calls this feature a state, but the evidence supports a culture or people label with major uncertainty. No source documents a single Charrúa capital, dynasty, bureaucracy, census, or surveyed frontier matching the polygon. The override therefore corrects kind and explains the atlas umbrella openly.

Colonial archives used changing ethnic names strategically and inconsistently. One study finds that Charrúa became a catchall for disparate peoples, while communities organized through distinct tolderías and networks of kinship, trade, and authority. A familiar national name cannot erase the atlas labels Bohanes and Guenoa-Muinanes or historically recorded Yaro, Chaná, and Guaraní identities.

The “Charrúa Complex” study treats labels as evidence to investigate, not boxes already solved. A name might be an autonym, an exonym, a subgroup, or a recorder’s confusion. Archaeology, documents, linguistics, and biological anthropology can constrain one another, but none makes the early map simple.

The National Museum’s regional archaeology summary lists mounds, ceramics, domesticated dogs, beans, squash, maize, and native plants. It deliberately describes numerous Indigenous groups. Those discoveries correct the stereotype of an empty or technologically simple land, while refusing the shortcut “found in Uruguay, therefore Charrúa.”

Two ancient genomes from the CH2D01-A mound date roughly 1,450 and 668 radiocarbon years before present. The study calls them Indigenous people of the region and says mound-to-historical-group relationships remain unresolved. Even DNA needs comparison samples, chronology, archaeology, and cautious language.

A modern genomic study sequenced ten volunteers with varied self-reported Indigenous ancestry. Its authors place “Charrúa” in quotation marks because exact ancestry is uncertain and neighboring Chaná and Minuán reference samples are missing. Genetic ancestry, community identity, and one historical nation are related questions, not interchangeable answers.

sections.title: Live in varied landscapes and settlements

items.text: Tamanduá rockshelter preserves separated visits from the early Holocene into historical times, including a roughly 3,000-year-old relationship with nearby mound landscapes and later Guaraní pottery. A shelter can host many occupations. Stratigraphy and radiocarbon dates keep those visits from becoming one timeless Charrúa household.

At García Ricci, nine mounds vary in size and height. The tallest, over four metres, began more than 4,000 years ago; smaller one-to-two-metre mounds were raised within the last 2,500 years. The booklet presents them as earth architecture, while their builders’ later historical name remains unresolved.

Upper Paraná Delta mounds combine elevated living places, burials, food remains, and evidence discussed as horticulture. Researchers debate hierarchy and settlement organization. This proves regional wetland societies could build durable places, but it cannot supply a Charrúa king, class system, or identical village plan across the atlas polygon.

At García Ricci in northern Rocha, nine mounds differ in height and age. Their fill includes local earth, burned anthill or termite-mound soil, animal bone, fish, pottery fragments, stone-working waste, and hearth remains. A mound could be architecture and an archive, though its builders’ historical name is unresolved.

A late eighteenth-century outsider description, compiled after its observer arrived in the Río de la Plata in 1782, says women bent three or four green poles, covered the arches with cattle hide, and made a toldo for a couple and some children. It offers comparison, not a 1492 floor plan.

sections.title: Find food without inventing one menu

items.text: Museum evidence from an 18-centimetre coiled pot uses soot and residues to test cooking and storage. Comparable regional vessels could prepare fish, store plant foods, ferment drinks, or serve ritual and funerary purposes. A pot can hold dinner and archaeology’s clues, but it cannot name its maker’s people.

Middle Paraná researchers recovered maize, bean, and squash microremains from dental calculus, burial sediments, and vessels alongside fishing and hunting evidence. Microscopic starch and phytoliths reveal plants that bones overlook. The assemblages show regional mixed foodways without proving that every household farmed or ate the same meal.

At mound site CH2D01, flotation and experimental work recovered 840 pieces of charcoal. Identified plants included Butiá and Pindó palms and several new regional archaeological records. Charred wood and seeds can reveal fuel and valued plants, but they do not preserve a complete supper or its cook’s name.

A museum teaching pot from Montevideo was built with clay coils and retains soot outside. Comparable regional vessels held fish, stored plants, or fermented drinks. Residue analysis can test what touched a pot; soot cannot tell whether dinner was delicious, although somebody probably had an opinion.

Animal bones, fish, burned palm fruits, pottery, hearths, and shaped landscapes show food work across different regional sites. Each clue preserves a different activity and date. Combining them is stronger than repeating a colonial claim that everyone lived only by hunting, yet none becomes automatically Charrúa.

Bolas joined one, two, or three stone, bone, or metal weights with cords of sinew, hide, or plant fiber. They could serve hunting or fighting. Museum researchers studied 290 possible examples from 13 Uruguayan departments, but poor provenience and long chronologies prevent assigning every round stone to Charrúa makers.

Making a grooved stone ball could require choosing a blank, pecking it toward shape, smoothing or polishing the surface, and cutting a groove. Similar rounded objects may instead be net weights, unfinished pieces, or recycled tools. Archaeologists inspect manufacture and context before letting a sphere become a boleadora.

A deer-bone awl from Cañada Saldaña was fractured or sawn from a strong leg bone and sharpened by abrasion; some bone tools were heated. Such points could pierce hides, mark pottery, or work basketry. Repeated resharpening shortened them, rather like a pencil that eventually becomes a stub.

At Los Cardos, makers fractured, hammered, abraded, and drilled freshwater shells into small circular beads. Groups of beads suggest necklaces or attachment to clothing. The museum carefully says “probably,” because a central hole supports suspension but cannot recover the wearer, occasion, social meaning, or historical ethnic name.

A polished slate object from Canelones has a hole near one end and is traditionally called a pendant. Its original function remains unknown, and comparable finds are scarce. Good archaeology can describe its thin shape, material, polish, and perforation while leaving “jewelry” as a possibility rather than a fact.

sections.title: Meet families and social worlds cautiously

items.text: A late eighteenth-century outsider account, compiled after its observer arrived in 1782, reports household-sized hide toldos and evening meetings of male family heads about watches, travel, hunting, camp movement, defense, and disputes. Participants could decline proposals without formal punishment. It suggests persuasion and household autonomy, not 1492 politics.

A historical study documents that women and children survived the Salsipuedes attack, were taken prisoner, and were distributed as servile labor among Montevideo families. This was forced family separation by the Uruguayan state. Descendants make “extinction” language especially misleading, even when organized communities were violently broken apart.

A memory study says descendants’ collective memories circulated outside public view, in private settings, before later organizations brought alternative accounts into public debate. In explaining such transmission, it discusses family settings, associations, and networks of affective or political sociability. This is evidence about memory, not reconstructed 1492 household rules.

Uruguay’s human-rights institution names women’s organizations and describes Indigenous women leading cultural, political, and neighborhood education work. Its census figures cover Indigenous ancestry broadly, not Charrúa alone. The modern evidence shows active social life while warning readers against turning a national percentage into one people’s headcount.

The archive study reconstructs later tolderías as extended networks of kinship, trade, and political authority, but it does not securely recover 1492 Charrúa marriage rules, birth customs, inheritance, or child-rearing routines. That scoped gap protects families from a made-up universal rule and leaves room for variation between communities.

sections.title: Learn, remember, and read one later word

items.text: No secure Charrúa-authored sentence or alphabet is documented for 1492 to 1500. The language study says usable records associated with Charrúa date to the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. This writing gap does not mean people lacked speech, stories, names, teaching, memory, diplomacy, or detailed environmental knowledge.

Written sample from a November 1842 manuscript: “hué”; the editor adds the reading “[we]”; the Spanish gloss is “agua,” meaning “water.” This is a collector’s alphabetic notation from a later informant, not an original 1492 inscription, and the bracketed form is editorial guidance rather than a full transliteration system.

Vilardebó’s two manuscripts drew on an army sergeant who had lived among Charrúa people and a woman said to know the language. They were first published in 1937. The surviving total is only a few dozen words, some doubtful, with no grammar or proper dictionary.

A 2025 public film forum brought Charrúa and Chaná community representatives, filmmakers, specialists, and audiences together. Basquadé Inchalá members discussed a collaboratively shaped story, and organizers planned educational circulation. Learning here happens through conversation, creative work, community authority, film, and classrooms, all clearly modern.

Indigenous women’s organizations in Uruguay promote culture and traditions through neighborhood educational processes and public advocacy. That official account names ADENCH, Clan Chonik, CONACHA, Descendientes de Charrúas de Flores, and others. Children can therefore meet living organizers, not only a textbook’s tragic final page.

sections.title: Discuss health, care, and missing evidence

items.text: A late eighteenth-century outsider account, compiled after its observer arrived in 1782, reports healers using forceful sucking at a patient’s stomach and receiving gifts. The writer made sweeping, prejudiced claims, and another observer later criticized his language knowledge and access to camps. This documents a report, not one timeless medical system.

The CH2D01-A mound held primary and secondary burials of at least 21 people; two provided low-coverage whole genomes. Those data illuminate ancestry and burial context. They do not recover pain treatment, childbirth care, infant feeding, disability support, elder care, or the cause of every death.

Food residues and human isotopes at Cerritos sites can compare fish, plants, and dietary histories, but the researchers say preservation limits demographic and individual health reconstruction. A cooking pot can disclose fish fat with impressive chemistry; it still cannot diagnose the cook or describe bedside care.

Modern genome research found Indigenous ancestry in participating Uruguayans while stressing uncertain historical labels and limited comparison samples. DNA is not a medical chart or a cultural membership test. It cannot prove that one remedy worked, identify a healer, or decide who belongs to a living Charrúa community.

The Cerritos pottery study says scarce human remains limit even basic demographic and individual health reconstruction. It does not recover pregnancy, birth, infant illness, disability support, elder care, or epidemic response for named Charrúa communities. That is a bounded evidence gap, not proof that families lacked care.

sections.title: Follow water, fire, waste, and sanitation evidence

items.text: Wetlands presented engineering challenges. Reviewed mounds served as house platforms, funerary or ceremonial places, cultivation surfaces, territorial markers, and parts of village clusters. Their roles changed across centuries. Elevation reduced flood exposure, but archaeology does not describe one Charrúa drainage authority or civic water system.

A study of India Muerta and Paso Barranca proposes repeated earth-oven use as a major mound-building process. It examines archaeological signatures, whether ovens could raise mounds, and possible plant foods. In this interpretation, centuries of routine food processing gradually made higher ground: everyday cooking became construction without a master plan.

The García Ricci booklet describes nine mounds built from surrounding earth, burned anthill or termite-mound soil, and domestic refuse: hunted-animal and fish bones, dog remains, pottery fragments, stone-tool debris, and hearth remains. These are construction materials in that booklet, not evidence of a named Charrúa rubbish or sanitation system.

The museum’s ceramic sheet documents an 18-centimetre pot, coil manufacture, soot, and residue studies, with possible cooking, storage, fermentation, ritual, and funerary uses. It does not describe piped water, sewers, or standardized washing facilities. That scoped silence cannot define sanitation for every named 1492 community.

The museum panels explain durable ceramics, manufacture, domestic containers with soot, symbolic figures, and funerary urns. They do not identify a named 1492 Charrúa toilet, latrine, sewer, rubbish schedule, or bathing rule. The honest bathroom fact is limited to that reviewed evidence: those practices remain unresolved.

Researchers measured mound axes and local horizons to test astronomical patterning. Repeated orientations may reflect planning, seasons, or sky relationships, but geometry alone cannot name a constellation or priest. The achievement securely visible is deliberate, long-term landscape design paired with modern methods that test rather than assume.

Tubular Paraná Basin pottery lacks ordinary cooking residues and is awkward for domestic use. Microscopy, chemistry, context, and historical comparison support a mortuary interpretation. The vessels show specialized ceramic choices, while the study does not authorize one Charrúa afterlife doctrine for every community under the atlas color.

An Isla Larga burial used a large painted ceramic vessel, stone covering, and a second vessel as lid. Glass beads show complex sixteenth or seventeenth-century contact, and the museum attributes the urn practice to Tupí-Guaraní or Guaranized groups. Keeping that attribution prevents a beautiful object from being mislabeled Charrúa.

Uruguay’s Law 18.589 declares every 11 April the Day of the Charrúa Nation and Indigenous Identity. Public commemoration does not repair every historical harm, but it makes state memory, education, and debate visible. The law belongs to modern Uruguay and cannot retroactively validate the atlas boundary.

Argentina’s Indigenous affairs authority registered the legal personality of the Naybu community, belonging to the Charrúa people, in rural Colonia Federal, Entre Ríos. This official record demonstrates transborder living community organization. Modern legal recognition is continuity evidence, not proof that the 1492 polygon was an exact national territory.

ending.text: The atlas ends the exact Charrúa feature at 1500 because its software categories change. It does not record a battle, surrender, demographic collapse, or disappearance in that year. Later history must keep its own dates. The official Salsipuedes memory-site account describes the Uruguayan state attack of 1831, the displacement and enslavement of survivors, and four captives sent to Paris for public display. It also records community petitioners and the 2021 declaration of the place as a Site of Memory. These events violently disrupted organized communities and public visibility, but they occurred more than three centuries after the atlas seam. Present continuity is documented in a narrower way by the Consejo de la Nación Charrúa’s own site. CoNaCha says it was created in 2005, includes several communities in Uruguay, undertakes community activities, announced an itinerant intercultural school, and marked its twentieth anniversary together. Those statements establish living organization on that source’s terms; they do not turn the broad 1492 polygon into a surveyed national territory. The responsible ending is continuity across a cartographic seam: the atlas layer stops, while later Charrúa memory and organized community life remain visible in separately dated sources.
